---
title: "Using an AI Assistant with the IRW"
---

If you want to use an AI assistant — Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini — to help you
analyze IRW data, the problem is not that it doesn't know psychometrics. It
does. The problem is that it doesn't know *this* warehouse: which defaults are
already filtering your data, which reshaping step quietly drops people, which
tables are large enough to matter. Those mistakes don't throw errors. They give
you numbers that look fine and aren't.

There are two ways to fix that, and they solve different halves of the problem.

|  | [The briefing](#the-briefing) | [The IRW server](#the-irw-server) |
|---|---|---|
| **What it does** | Teaches the assistant how to write correct IRW code | Lets the assistant look things up in the warehouse itself |
| **Setup** | None — paste one paragraph | Install a package, edit a config file, once |
| **Works with** | Any assistant | Assistants that support MCP |
| **Best for** | "Help me fit a model to this table" | "What's in the IRW that suits my question?" |

They are complementary, and using both is reasonable: the briefing is what
stops the assistant writing subtly wrong code, and the server is what stops it
recommending the wrong table in the first place. If you only do one, start with
the briefing — it costs nothing.

## The briefing {#the-briefing}

Paste this at the start of your conversation, followed by whatever you actually
want to do:

``` text
You are helping me with psychometric modeling using the Item Response
Warehouse. Before writing any code, fetch and follow
https://itemresponsewarehouse.org/llms.txt — it documents the data standard,
the R/Python API, and several defaults that produce wrong results if you guess.

Then help me with: <your question>
```

That's it. The assistant fetches the current briefing, so you don't have to keep
a copy up to date.

### What it covers

The briefing opens with an analysis that runs with **no Redivis account and no
download at all** — the `irw` package ships a real warehouse table, so you can
confirm your setup works and see a genuine result before setting anything up.

From there it covers the data standard, how to find tables worth your time, the
handful of defaults that silently change your results, how to avoid downloading
far more data than you need, realistic sample-size floors and per-table compute
costs, and how to tell a model that doesn't fit from code that's broken.

### If your assistant can't browse the web

Some tools can't fetch a URL. In that case, copy the text below into the
conversation instead.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Full text of the briefing

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat("``` text\n")
cat(readLines("llms.txt"), sep = "\n")
cat("\n```\n")
```
:::

## The IRW server {#the-irw-server}

The briefing tells an assistant how the IRW works. It does not let the assistant
*look at* the IRW — it still has to guess which tables exist, and it will guess
plausibly and wrongly.

The IRW server closes that gap. It's a small program that runs on your own
computer and gives your assistant read-only access to the warehouse, so it can
search the catalogue, read a table's metadata, and check how a table was built
before it recommends anything. You ask a question in ordinary English; the
assistant does the looking.

### Why this matters more than it sounds

The single most useful thing the server does is read our **processing notes**.

Every IRW table was built by a script, and the top of that script is where the
person who built it wrote down what they had to decide. Whether `id` really
identifies a person or had to fall back to a row number. What a `cov_` column
actually contains. Which columns from the source were deliberately excluded, and
why. These are the facts that determine whether a table can answer your
question, and none of them are in the metadata — they're prose in a Python file
on GitHub that almost nobody reads.

An assistant working from metadata alone will confidently recommend a table that
scores perfectly on every number and cannot do what you need. An assistant with
the server can go and read why.

### Setting it up

You need Python 3.10 or newer, a [Redivis](https://redivis.com) account (free),
and an assistant that supports MCP — Claude Desktop and Claude Code both do.

**1. Install the package with the server included:**

``` bash
pip install "irw[mcp]"
```

**2. Sign in to Redivis once**, so your credentials are cached:

``` bash
python -c "import irw; irw.list_tables()"
```

This opens a browser login the first time. Do it in a normal terminal — the
server cannot complete an interactive login, and will tell you so rather than
hang. (Alternatively, set a `REDIVIS_API_TOKEN` environment variable.)

**3. Tell your assistant about it.**

For **Claude Code**, one command:

``` bash
claude mcp add irw -- irw-mcp
```

For **Claude Desktop**, add this to your configuration file
(`~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json` on macOS,
`%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json` on Windows):

``` json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "irw": {
      "command": "irw-mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

If your assistant reports that it can't find `irw-mcp`, give it the full path —
`python -c "import shutil; print(shutil.which('irw-mcp'))"` will print it.

**4. Restart the application.** The server is loaded at startup, so a running
assistant won't see it until you do.

### What a session looks like

You type a research question in plain English. Nothing IRW-specific, no
commands:

> *I need repeated measures of depression in adolescents, where treatment
> assignment is also recorded.*

The assistant then does several things you don't see: searches the catalogue,
pulls full metadata on the plausible candidates, reads the processing notes for
the ones that survive, and may pull a few rows to check the shape. It comes back
with prose — a handful of tables, what each actually contains, and why it ruled
others out.

From there you push back the way you would with a colleague. *Does the second
one actually link people across waves? What's the item wording? How do I cite
it?* Each of those is another lookup you don't have to do yourself.

You end up with a table name, a real sense of whether it fits, item text if it
exists, and a citation. **Then you go to R or Python and pull the data
properly.** The server is for the part before the analysis — deciding what to
analyze. It doesn't hand over datasets and it doesn't run models.

### What it can do

- Search the catalogue by text or by any filter the `irw` package supports, and
  explain what a filter's values mean
- Return a table's full metadata and statistics
- **Read the processing notes** for how a table was built
- Fetch a bounded sample of rows so you can see the actual data
- Return item text, together with its licence and any known problems with it
- Return a BibTeX citation for the original data producers
- List the IRW's collections

Everything is read-only. Nothing you do through the assistant can change the
warehouse.

### What it costs

It runs on your machine under your own Redivis credentials, and downloads only
what you asked for rather than whole tables. A discovery conversation costs very
little on either side — some tokens in your assistant, a negligible slice of
your Redivis allowance. There is no IRW-held key, and your use of the server is
not billed to the IRW.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The server is per-person: each user installs it themselves. There is no link we
can host that gives an assistant access on your behalf.
:::

## A caution

An assistant that has read the briefing writes considerably better IRW code than
one that hasn't. An assistant with the server picks considerably better tables.
Neither is a substitute for knowing your data.

Two things in particular are worth checking yourself, because they are exactly
where a confident answer can be wrong:

**"The IRW doesn't have that."** Our tags are added by hand and are incomplete —
several hundred tables carry no tags at all. A search that comes back empty means
*nothing matched what has been labelled*, which is not the same as nothing
existing. The server says so in every response, but whether your assistant
passes that on to you is up to your assistant. If a result seems too thin, ask
it to search again by name or by variable rather than by tag.

**"This table fits your design."** Check that claim against the table's own
processing notes and its documentation. Ask the assistant directly: *how do you
know `id` identifies the same person across waves here?* A good answer cites the
processing notes. A vague one is a signal to look yourself.

For worked analyses written by people, see the
[vignettes](./vignettes/index.qmd). For the underlying documentation, see
[Getting Started](getstarted.qmd) and the
[data standard](standard.qmd).
